content: 1. A comprehensive meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the relationship between active commuting and all-cause mortality, as well as the incidence and mortality of cardiovascular diseases, cancer, and diabetes. The analysis included data from 23 prospective cohort studies with a total of 531,333 participants. The results indicated that active commuting was associated with a significantly reduced risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease incidence, and diabetes. However, no significant association was found between active commuting and cardiovascular disease mortality or cancer. 2. A systematic review and harmonized meta-analysis were performed to examine the dose-response relationships between accelerometer-measured physical activity, sedentary time, and all-cause mortality. Data were sourced from PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, Web of Science, and SportDiscus up to July 31, 2018. The analysis included prospective cohort studies that assessed physical activity and sedentary time using accelerometry. The findings revealed that any level of physical activity, regardless of intensity, was associated with a lower risk of mortality, with a non-linear dose-response relationship. Higher levels of physical activity and reduced sedentary time were linked to substantially lower risks of premature mortality, particularly in middle-aged and older adults. 3. A systematic review investigated the association between leisure-time physical activity during adulthood and domain-specific cognitive functions in older adults (aged 60+ years). The review included 23 studies (9 cross-sectional and 14 longitudinal) and found that moderateand vigorous-intensity leisure physical activity was positively associated with global cognitive function, executive functions, and memory, but not attention or working memory. Most studies focused on mid-to-late adulthood physical activity, with limited data on the influence of physical activity during young adulthood. The evidence supports the beneficial role of leisure physical activity in maintaining cognitive functions during old age. 4. A meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessed the effects of resistance exercise training (RET) on anxiety symptoms. The analysis included 31 effect sizes from 16 studies involving 922 participants. RET significantly improved anxiety symptoms in both healthy individuals and those with physical or mental illnesses. The improvements were not moderated by sex or specific features of the RET intervention. Future trials should compare RET with other empirically supported therapies for anxiety to further validate its efficacy. 5. Another meta-analysis examined the association between resistance exercise training (RET) and depressive symptoms. The analysis included 33 RCTs with 1,877 participants. RET significantly reduced depressive symptoms across various populations, regardless of health status, total prescribed RET volume, or strength improvements. However, smaller reductions in depressive symptoms were observed in trials with blinded allocation and assessment. The findings highlight the need for high-quality RCTs to further explore the antidepressant effects of RET and compare it with other treatments for depression. 6. A systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the influence of physical activity at a young age and lifetime physical activity on the risks of obesity-related cancers, including breast, colon, and endometrial cancers. The analysis followed MOOSE guidelines and included observational studies. Physical activity during middle and late adulthood was strongly associated with reduced risks of these cancers. However, the evidence for the protective effects of physical activity during childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood (ages 5–30 years) remains limited. Further research is needed to clarify the role of early-life physical activity in cancer prevention.
